nameStory: This tiny jellyfish gets its scientific name from Norwegian marine biologist Michael Sars, who first described many Arctic marine species in the 1800s. The species name 'tubulosa' refers to the tubular shape of its polyp stage, when it looks like a tiny tube attached to rocks or seaweed before transforming into the free-swimming bell form we recognize as a jellyfish.
description: Sarsia tubulosa is a delicate, transparent jellyfish about the size of a marble - rarely growing larger than half an inch across. It has a crystal-clear, dome-shaped bell with four long, thread-like tentacles that can extend several times the bell's diameter. This tiny marine wanderer belongs to the bell jellies, a group of small jellyfish that drift through coastal waters. Despite its diminutive size, it's a capable predator that pulses gracefully through the water column.

idTips.label: Bell shape and size
idTips.description: Clear, dome-shaped bell about the size of a marble or smaller, completely transparent like glass with a firm, rubbery texture when touched

idTips.label: Four long tentacles
idTips.description: Exactly four thread-like tentacles that can stretch out like fishing lines, much longer than the bell width and incredibly thin

idTips.label: Central mouth tube
idTips.description: A prominent tube-like mouth (manubrium) hanging down from the center of the bell, often reddish or orange in color

idTips.label: Swimming motion
idTips.description: Distinctive pulsing rhythm as it contracts and expands its bell, moving in a jerky up-and-down pattern through the water

idTips.label: Tentacle positioning
idTips.description: Tentacles emerge from four equally-spaced points around the bell margin, often trailing behind as it swims

habitat: Found in cool coastal waters of New England, particularly in harbors, bays, and nearshore areas where the water temperature stays relatively cold. They prefer areas with good water circulation and are often spotted near docks, piers, or rocky shores where their polyp stage can attach to hard surfaces.

seasonality.spring: Adult medusae begin appearing in coastal waters as temperatures start to rise, though still quite rare to spot.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for observing the free-swimming jellyfish stage in New England waters, especially in cooler coastal areas and harbors.
seasonality.fall: Numbers typically decline as water temperatures drop, though some individuals may persist into early autumn.
seasonality.winter: Adult medusae are absent from the water column, existing only as tiny polyps attached to underwater surfaces.

funFact: This tiny jellyfish has two completely different body forms during its lifetime - it starts as a tube-shaped polyp stuck to a rock that looks nothing like a jellyfish, then buds off miniature medusae that swim away, essentially cloning itself to spread throughout the ocean.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other small, transparent jellyfish, but the combination of exactly four long tentacles and the prominent central mouth tube distinguishes it from most other bell jellies. Remember: 'Four fishing lines from a glass marble' - that's your Sarsia.
contextualKnowledge: Note: With only 4 recorded observations in New England, this species is quite rare in our waters and represents the northern edge of its range. Most sightings of small transparent jellyfish in New England waters are likely other species, making any Sarsia tubulosa encounter particularly noteworthy.
compareHints: Since this is the only Sarsia species recorded in New England waters, compare it to other small bell jellies in the Corynidae family by counting tentacles carefully - many related species have different numbers of tentacles or shorter tentacles relative to their bell size. The prominent, tube-like mouth structure is also more developed in Sarsia than in many of its cousins.
